Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: The threat items are oriented toward external environmental danger (scanning surroundings, planning escape routes), which is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 68-year-old policy analyst unless there is an additional trauma context not represented here.

Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance reinforces an expectation of unpredictable external danger, which fits assault/combat-type trauma more than illness trauma and does not cohere well with the rest of the illness-based profile.

Memory: Guilt on Recall and Negative Appraisals: Character Blame imply a strong self-blame/guilt formulation, but the other selected items center on current danger vigilance and emotional loss; for life-threatening illness, this specific self-blame pattern is possible but, combined with the external-danger threat items, creates a clinically incoherent mix of trauma themes.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, persistent escape-route scanning is hard to reconcile with the trauma context. It implies imminent external attack or entrapment rather than illness-related threat, while the rest of the profile centers on bodily danger and emotional change.

Intense guilt on recall is not impossible after severe illness, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile: the appraisals focus on permanent emotional loss and bodily alarm rather than responsibility for causing harm or failing others. The guilt theme lacks support elsewhere in memory or appraisals.

'The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am' suggests a strong characterological self-blame formulation. In a life-threatening illness case, that can occur, but in this profile it is not well integrated with the other selected appraisals, which focus on bodily danger and emotional numbing. Together with guilt on recall, it introduces a self-blame theme that is otherwise unsupported.

vignette: Kofi had always taken pride in his sharp mind and quick wit. As a policy analyst for over three decades, he was used to digging through complex data and crafting sound recommendations. But all of that changed two years ago when he received the devastating diagnosis: stage IV prostate cancer. The words still echoed in his mind like a death sentence. The treatment that followed was grueling – rounds of chemotherapy, radiation, and endless doctor's appointments. Kofi tried to stay focused on his work, but it became increasingly difficult to concentrate. His mind would wander back to the hospital room where he received the diagnosis, reliving the moment when his whole world came crashing down. Even now, as he sat in his living room, trying to read a report or watch TV, he found himself drifting away, his thoughts hijacked by the memory of that fateful day. Sometimes, Kofi would recall the details of his treatment with an eerie detachment – feeling like he was observing someone else's life. Other times, the memories came flooding back in vivid, terrifying detail. He'd be sitting at home when suddenly he was back in the hospital bed, surrounded by beeping machines and antiseptic smells, his body wracked with pain. The memory felt so real, so present, that Kofi would have to stop whatever he was doing, overcome by a wave of emotion. Kofi's body had become his greatest enemy. Even now, long after the treatment had ended, it still reacted as if danger lurked around every corner. His muscles remained tense and coiled, ready to spring into action at the slightest provocation. He'd catch himself holding his breath or flinching at a sudden noise – an innocuous sound that, in another life, would have passed unnoticed. At home, Kofi felt like he was walking on eggshells, waiting for the other shoe to drop. He couldn't shake the feeling that something was off, even when everything seemed fine. He'd wake up in the middle of the night, his heart racing, with no clear reason why. His body had betrayed him once; Kofi wasn't sure he could ever trust it again. The numbness he felt – not just about his emotions but also about life itself – terrified Kofi. Would he ever be able to feel normal emotions again? Or would this flatline continue indefinitely, a constant reminder of the fragility of his own mortality? He longed for the days when laughter came easily and tears didn't seem like an existential threat. Kofi's work began to suffer as well. Colleagues noticed a change in him – a once-sharp mind now dulled by distraction and anxiety. Projects piled up, deadlines loomed, and Kofi found himself unable to concentrate on even the simplest tasks. His confidence waned; his sense of self-worth dwindled. It was only when he realized that his grandchildren were starting to notice the change in him – their once-vibrant grandfather now a shadow of his former self – that Kofi finally sought help. He knew he couldn't keep living like this, trapped in a world where memories haunted him and his body felt like a minefield waiting to be triggered. As he sat in his therapist's office for the first time, Kofi felt a glimmer of hope – maybe, just maybe, there was a way out of this labyrinth. But what scared him most was the thought that it might already be too late, that the damage had been done and all he could do now was try to pick up the pieces of a life forever shattered by illness and fear.
